title: Chemical Bonding
summary: The noble gases (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon) hardly form compounds. Except helium (2 electrons), they all have 8 electrons in their outermost shell, which is a very stable arrangement. Other atoms combine with each other to reach this noble-gas configuration — 8 electrons in the outer shell (2 for hydrogen, like helium). This tendency is called the octet rule and is the basic cause of chemical bonding. A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms together; bond formation lowers the energy, so the compound is more stable than the separate atoms. Atoms reach an octet either by transferring electrons (ionic bond) or by sharing them (covalent bond).

An ionic bond is formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. Sodium (2,8,1) loses its one outer electron to become the sodium cation Na⁺ (2,8 — like neon). Chlorine (2,8,7) gains that electron to become the chloride anion Cl⁻ (2,8,8 — like argon). The oppositely charged ions are held together by the strong electrostatic (Coulombic) force of attraction — the ionic bond: 2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl. Losing an electron needs energy (496 kJ/mol for Na) and gaining one releases energy (349 kJ/mol for Cl); the extra energy released when the ions pack into a crystal makes NaCl stable.

In solid sodium chloride each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions and each Cl⁻ by six Na⁺ ions, in a regular three-dimensional crystal lattice; there are no separate NaCl molecules, and NaCl is only the formula showing one Na⁺ for every Cl⁻. Similarly, magnesium (2,8,2) loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺: with two chlorine atoms it forms MgCl2, and with an oxygen atom (2,6 → O²⁻, 2,8) it forms magnesium oxide, MgO.

(a) They are crystalline solids, hard and brittle. (b) They have high melting and boiling points (NaCl melts at 801 °C and boils at 1413 °C) because much energy is needed to overcome the strong forces between ions. (c) They do not conduct electricity in the solid state, where ions are fixed in the lattice, but conduct when molten or dissolved in water, because the ions become free to move. (d) They are generally soluble in water but insoluble in organic solvents such as alcohol, ether and carbon tetrachloride (a few, like barium sulphate, silver chloride and calcium fluoride, are insoluble in water).

A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of electron pairs between two atoms, usually non-metals; each atom contributes equally. In H2 each hydrogen shares its one electron, so both get two electrons like helium: H–H. The bond forms at the distance where attraction and repulsion balance and the energy is lowest.

Single, double and triple bonds: in Cl2 each chlorine (2,8,7) shares one electron — one shared pair, a single bond (Cl–Cl). In O2 each oxygen (2,6) shares two electrons — two shared pairs, a double bond (O=O). In N2 each nitrogen (2,5) shares three electrons — three shared pairs, a triple bond (N≡N). Different atoms can also share: in HCl hydrogen and chlorine share one pair, so H has 2 and Cl has 8 outer electrons; water has two O–H single bonds. Diagrams that show only the outer electrons as dots or crosses are called Lewis (electron-dot) structures.

They are made of neutral molecules held by weak intermolecular forces, so: (a) they may be gases (O2, N2, CO2), liquids (water, CCl4) or solids (iodine, naphthalene); (b) they have low melting and boiling points (naphthalene melts at 80 °C, CCl4 boils at 77 °C); (c) they do not conduct electricity because they have no ions or free electrons — ethyl alcohol does not conduct even in water; (d) they are generally insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as alcohol, benzene and ether (iodine dissolves in alcohol to form tincture of iodine).

case.passage: Atoms combine to attain the stable configuration of the nearest noble gas. A metal such as sodium (2,8,1) gives its outer electron to a non-metal such as chlorine (2,8,7); the ions formed are held by electrostatic attraction in a crystal lattice. Non-metal atoms such as two chlorine atoms, or hydrogen and chlorine, complete their octets by sharing pairs of electrons, forming molecules. Ionic compounds have high melting points and conduct when molten; covalent compounds have low melting points and do not conduct.

vsa: Why do noble gases not take part in chemical reactions?
Noble gases already have a stable configuration — 8 electrons in the outermost shell (helium has 2). They have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons, so they do not react.
Why are ionic compounds good conductors of electricity in the molten state but bad conductors in the solid state?

In the solid state the ions are held in fixed positions in the crystal lattice and cannot move. On melting (or dissolving in water) the lattice breaks and the ions become free to move, so they carry current.
Write two differences between ionic and covalent compounds.

(1) Ionic compounds are hard crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points; covalent compounds may be gases, liquids or solids with low melting and boiling points. (2) Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in water and dissolve in water; covalent compounds do not conduct and usually dissolve in organic solvents.
How many covalent bonds are present in H2O, HCl, O2 and N2?
H2O: 2 (two O–H single bonds); HCl: 1; O2: 2 (a double bond); N2: 3 (a triple bond).
Explain the formation of the Na⁺ ion from a sodium atom.

Sodium (Z = 11) has configuration 2, 8, 1. It loses its single outer electron: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻. The ion has 11 protons and 10 electrons, so it has one positive charge, and its configuration 2, 8 is like that of neon.
Why are covalent compounds poor conductors of electricity?
Covalent compounds are made of electrically neutral molecules. They have no ions or free electrons to carry charge, so they do not conduct electricity even in solution (e.g. ethyl alcohol).
sa: Element X has atomic number 11 and element Y has atomic number 17. (a) Write the electronic configuration of both. (b) Which type of bond will form between X and Y? (c) Write the formula of the compound formed.
(a) X (sodium): 2, 8, 1; Y (chlorine): 2, 8, 7. (b) X loses one electron and Y gains it, so an ionic (electrovalent) bond forms between X⁺ and Y⁻. (c) XY, i.e. NaCl.

An element A has atomic number 12 and element B has atomic number 8. (a) What type of bond will they form? Give reason. (b) Explain the electrical conductivity of the compound formed.

(a) A (magnesium, 2,8,2) loses two electrons to become A²⁺ and B (oxygen, 2,6) gains them to become B²⁻; this transfer forms an ionic bond, giving AB (MgO). (b) Being ionic, it does not conduct in the solid state (ions fixed) but conducts when molten (ions free to move).
October 2022
How is a covalent bond formed? Explain the formation of the oxygen molecule. Why are covalent compounds poor conductors of electricity?

A covalent bond forms when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons so that each completes its octet. Each oxygen atom (2,6) needs two electrons; the two atoms share two pairs of electrons, forming a double bond (O=O), and each now has 8 outer electrons. Covalent compounds consist of neutral molecules with no ions or free electrons, so they cannot carry current.
April 2023
Explain the formation of the covalent bond between hydrogen and chlorine to form HCl. Write two properties of covalent substances.

Hydrogen (1) needs one electron to have 2, and chlorine (2,8,7) needs one to have 8. Each gives one electron to form a shared pair, H–Cl, a single covalent bond; H now has 2 and Cl has 8 outer electrons. Properties: low melting and boiling points; do not conduct electricity; usually insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
April 2019
Write two differences between the properties of ionic and covalent compounds. Give two examples of each.

(1) Ionic compounds are hard crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points; covalent compounds are often gases or liquids with low melting and boiling points. (2) Ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or in solution and dissolve in water; covalent compounds do not conduct and dissolve in organic solvents. Ionic: sodium chloride, magnesium oxide. Covalent: methane, hydrogen chloride (also water, CCl4).
October 2017
How is an ionic bond formed? Explain the formation of magnesium oxide.

An ionic bond forms when a metal atom transfers electrons to a non-metal atom and the oppositely charged ions attract each other. Magnesium (2,8,2) loses two electrons: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ (2,8). Oxygen (2,6) gains them: O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻ (2,8). Both ions now have the neon configuration and are held together by electrostatic attraction, forming MgO.

sa: Explain the process of covalent bond formation with an example. Identify the covalent bonds in N2, Cl2, O2 and HCl.

Two non-metal atoms each contribute electrons to form shared pairs, so that both complete their octet; e.g. two chlorine atoms (2,8,7) share one pair to form Cl–Cl. N2: triple bond (N≡N, 3 shared pairs); Cl2: single bond; O2: double bond (O=O); HCl: single bond (H–Cl).

la: Describe the formation of the ionic bond between sodium and chlorine atoms to form sodium chloride. Explain why the melting and boiling points of ionic compounds are higher than those of covalent compounds, and why sodium chloride conducts electricity when molten but not as a solid.

Sodium (2,8,1) loses its outer electron to form Na⁺ (2,8); chlorine (2,8,7) gains it to form Cl⁻ (2,8,8). Both reach noble-gas configurations, and the oppositely charged ions are held by a strong electrostatic force — the ionic bond (2Na + Cl2 → 2NaCl). In the crystal each Na⁺ is surrounded by six Cl⁻ and vice versa. A lot of energy is needed to break these strong forces between ions, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points; covalent compounds have only weak forces between molecules. In solid NaCl the ions are fixed and cannot move, so it does not conduct; when molten (or in water) the ions are free to move and carry current.
What is meant by (i) an ionic bond and (ii) a covalent bond? Compare ionic and covalent compounds with respect to physical state, conductivity and solubility.

(i) An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between ions formed by the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal (e.g. NaCl). (ii) A covalent bond is formed by the sharing of electron pairs between atoms (e.g. Cl2, HCl). Physical state: ionic compounds are hard crystalline solids; covalent compounds may be gases, liquids or soft solids. Conductivity: ionic compounds conduct when molten or dissolved, not as solids; covalent compounds do not conduct. Solubility: ionic compounds usually dissolve in water but not in organic solvents; covalent compounds usually dissolve in organic solvents but not in water.
